meta.regime: Yesterday's de-escalation trade was sold a story that Tehran spent Monday evening denying, and the second leg of the board - the yen - lost its fundamental support overnight. On the geopolitics: Trump called off the weekend strikes and said US-Iran talks would resume, and crude was marked down 7.4% to about $78 WTI on it, the sharpest single session of 2026. Iran's foreign ministry then contradicted him outright. Spokesman Baghaei: 'We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz.' Foreign Minister Araghchi told cabinet the Oman track is 'in their final stages' and 'on the way to being finalized' - but explicitly added that such an agreement 'did not mean the reopening of the strait.' So the direction of travel is still de-escalation, but the specific thing the oil market priced - a complete and total reopening negotiated directly with Washington - is not what is on the table. That makes the risk in USOIL two-way from here rather than one-way, and it means the whole chain that hangs off crude (CAD, NZD, the ECB's September hike pricing, gold) should not be pressed at these levels. On the yen: Japan's June labour cash earnings rose just 2.5% y/y against 3.2% expected, a clear miss and a direct hit to the wage-price cycle the BoJ says it needs. That matters because the yen's entire bid is now the joint MoF/US Treasury operation and the pledge to repeat it - the monetary leg has thinned out. Intervention is a level defence, not a trend, and a defended level without a rates story underneath is a fade risk once the operation goes quiet. Meanwhile the dollar found real support from data rather than fear: July ISM manufacturing jumped to 55.6 from 53.3 against a 54 consensus with new orders at 56.7, and although prices paid eased to 71.1 from 73 it remains deep in expansion. DXY is back at 99.90 pressing 100. The tell worth watching is that gold at $4,052 and silver at $58.26 both closed HIGHER against a firmer dollar - the metals complex is not buying the peace trade either.

dailyRead: Trade today as if the peace deal is smaller than Monday's price action implied, and as if the yen rally is more fragile than Monday's price action implied. Those are the two corrections the board needs. Iran's foreign ministry publicly denied the direct US negotiations Trump announced, limiting its own track to Oman-mediated talks on passage through the strait, and Araghchi said explicitly that a deal there does not equal reopening - yet WTI was marked down 7.4% to $78 anyway. The structural short in crude is still right, because the strait has been effectively shut since Feb 28 and traded below $70 when traffic briefly flowed in early July, but after a one-day 7.4% flush into an official denial the asymmetry has flipped: USOIL comes off SHORT HIGH to SHORT LOW-MED and should be managed, not added to, with a close back above $84 the invalidation. The same caution applies to everything that hangs off oil - do not press CAD shorts here, and note that the ECB's roughly 70% September hike pricing, which was built on the oil surge, only deflates if the reopening is real. On the yen, June labour cash earnings printed 2.5% y/y against 3.2% expected. That is the wage-price cycle the BoJ has made the precondition for its next hike, and it just came in soft, which is why JPY drops from +3 to +2 and the JPY-cross shorts come off HIGH to MED. The yen is now a pure intervention trade: the MoF and US Treasury acted jointly and said they would not hesitate again, USD/JPY sits near 156.90 having spiked to 155.39, and that keeps a hard ceiling on the pair - but it is a level defence with no rates engine under it, so take profit into strength rather than assuming trend. Where the trade is cleanest is the CHF block, because it is the one leg where the fundamentals and the flow agree: Swiss July CPI undershot again at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected with core stuck at 0.3%, sitting under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast, the policy rate is pinned at zero until 2027 and import prices are deflating at -2.1%. Long NZD/CHF and EUR/CHF, short CHF/JPY. The dollar earned its bid honestly for once - ISM manufacturing at 55.6 from 53.3 with new orders 56.7 beat comfortably and lifted yields - so USD/CAD LONG and AUD/USD SHORT are clean, while EUR/USD at 1.1510 and GBP/USD at 1.3430 are best left as RANGE into Friday's payrolls, which is the real gate on whether the three July FOMC dissenters get their September hike. Two events before then: NZ Q2 labour tonight at 22:45Z, where 5.4% unemployment is expected from 5.3% and which decides whether the RBNZ follows July's hike on Sept 2, and the RBA on Aug 11 where a hold is consensus but the Q2 weighted median rising to 3.7% keeps a hawkish tail alive for AUD shorts.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. The hawkish case got a real data point on Aug 3: July ISM manufacturing 55.6 from 53.3 against 54 consensus, new orders 56.7, prices paid 71.1. Against it: June CPI 3.5% with core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% advance and payrolls +57k. July jobs (Aug 7) and July CPI (Aug 12) decide it - a second sub-100k print kills the hike.

EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike (refi 2.40%, MLF 2.65%), confirmed unchanged at the Jul 23 meeting. June HICP 2.8%, core 2.4%, services 3.2%. The September pricing was built on the oil surge Lagarde flagged as an upside inflation risk - but Iran's denial that it is negotiating a reopening with Washington means that dovish repricing is far less certain than Monday's crude flush implied. Q1 GDP was 0.0% q/q, annual growth 0.3%.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6%, core 2.6%, services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3%, unemployment 4.9% - and July services PMI jumped to 51.8 from 48.8. The soft spot is manufacturing, revised down on Aug 3, which is why cable gave back its move to 1.3500.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (hike now looks Oct/Dec at best)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The wage leg just weakened materially: June labour cash earnings +2.5% y/y against +3.2% expected, after May slowed to 3.2% from 3.6%. That compounds a July Outlook Report that already CUT FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8%. The near-term yen driver is therefore fiscal, not monetary - a joint MoF/US Treasury operation with an explicit pledge to act again. June minutes are out Aug 4.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb, Mar, May) on the energy shock. Q2 trimmed mean 3.6% but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%. All four majors expect a hold; Finder's panel has 55% seeing at least one more 2026 hike and TE's model carries 4.60% for August. Cheaper crude and a softer commodity complex are what dragged AUD/USD back under 0.7000.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, with further increases described as possible. Q2 CPI 4.1% (petrol +27.5%), two-year inflation expectations 2.53%, ANZ business confidence 56.1. Tonight's Q2 labour report is the direct gate - 5.4% unemployment expected from 5.3%, employment +0.1% q/q, LCI +0.6% q/q. A soft print is what lets the Bank stand pat.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. June CPI cooled to 2.8% from 3.2% with CPI-trim 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, BOTH BELOW target, as gasoline decelerated to +20.5% y/y from +33.2%. Q1 GDP 0.0% q/q, -0.1% y/y. No rates leg at all - CAD is a pure terms-of-trade trade, and that is exactly what is being argued over in Muscat.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - that sits UNDER the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast, which Nomura flagged as a clear undershoot. Producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only; the SNB is content to let the franc slide.

catalysts.event: Iran DENIES negotiating with Washington — Oman-mediated Hormuz talks only, and not a reopening
catalysts.note: The most important correction on the board. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Baghaei: 'We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz.' Foreign Minister Araghchi told cabinet members that the Oman-mediated negotiations are 'in their final stages' and 'on the way to being finalized' but stated explicitly that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait. This directly contradicts Trump's claim of an imminent deal covering the 'Immediate, Complete and Total OPENING' of the strait - a claim that was the entire basis for Monday's 7.4% WTI collapse to $78 and the record DAX print. Background: the two sides signed an MoU in June allowing a 60-day temporary reopening and committing to nuclear talks; the strait has been effectively closed since the war began Feb 28. Direction of travel is still de-escalation, but the market priced the maximal version. This is the two-way swing factor over USOIL, XAU, CAD, NZD, GER40 and the entire CHF block.

catalysts.event: Joint US-Japan FX intervention — MoF pledges to act again
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed the MoF purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury and Treasury Secretary Bessent confirmed it from Washington, with both sides pledging not to hesitate on further joint action. USD/JPY spiked to 155.39 and trades near 156.90 against above 163 a week ago. Overt acknowledgement of coordinated intervention is rare - the last comparable case was 2011. But the fundamental support thinned overnight: June labour cash earnings printed +2.5% y/y against +3.2% expected. Size yen shorts for a second operation against you; size yen longs knowing there is now no rates engine underneath the level defence.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Q2 labour market report
catalysts.note: Consensus 5.4% unemployment from 5.3%, employment +0.1% q/q from +0.2%, labour cost index +0.6% q/q. This is the direct gate on whether the RBNZ follows July's first-in-three-years hike with another on Sept 2, and therefore on NZD/CHF, NZD/CAD, AUD/NZD, NZD/JPY and NZD/USD. Westpac expects the tick up to 5.4% with wage growth staying subdued.

The last read on labour demand before Friday's official report, and it carries extra weight this week because the three July FOMC dissenters need the labour market to hold up for a September hike to survive.

The biggest scheduled gate on the board. Consensus +91k after June's +57k, unemployment expected 4.3% from 4.2%, with April-May already revised down 74k combined. A second sub-100k print kills the September hike the three July dissenters want and breaks the dollar despite the ISM beat; a clean beat re-arms it and is the only credible counterweight to the joint yen intervention.

All four major Australian banks expect a hold at 4.35%, but the internals argue otherwise: the Q2 weighted median ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, and July PMIs printed six-month highs. Finder's panel has 55% of economists seeing at least one more 2026 hike and TE's model carries 4.60%. A hawkish statement is the live tail risk against AUD shorts.

TE forecasts 3.4% headline after June's 3.5%, with core last at 2.6%. Energy drove over 60% of a recent monthly gain, so whether the Hormuz premium actually comes out of crude feeds straight into this print and into the September FOMC decision. ISM prices paid at 71.1 says cost pressure is still in the pipeline.
Warsh's first Jackson Hole as Chair, and the venue where he would have to explain a September hike after refusing to give any guidance or submit a dot at the July press conference. Runs Aug 27-28.

TE models the OCR at 2.75% after July's move to 2.50%. But the Bank explicitly credited the partial Hormuz reopening with lowering oil and easing near-term inflation - so how tonight's labour data and the Oman track resolve decides whether this is a hike or a pause.

A seventh consecutive hold at 2.25% is the base case with CPI-trim 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, both under target. The interest is whether the Bank acknowledges that cheaper crude removes the energy contribution that has been holding headline CPI up at 2.8%.

Roughly 70% of a hike is priced, but that pricing was built on the oil surge Lagarde flagged as an upside inflation risk after officials had signalled patience at Sintra. With HICP 2.8%, core 2.4%, Q1 GDP flat q/q and annual growth 0.3%, cheaper crude is a direct dovish repricing risk - which is precisely why Iran's denial that a reopening is being negotiated matters for the euro.

CME FedWatch carries roughly 56-61% of a hike, TE nearer 77%, off the three July dissents and now an ISM at 55.6 - but July jobs and July CPI both land first, and Warsh has refused to pre-commit or submit a dot.

TE forecasts a hold at 3.75%, but the Jul 30 vote was 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus and July services PMI swung back into expansion at 51.8. A fourth dissenter would confirm sterling's hawkish tail; the downwardly revised manufacturing PMI is the counterargument.

A hold at 1.00% is now the firm base case - the July Outlook Report cut FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8% and June wages missed at 2.5% against 3.2% expected - with Oct/Dec the live meeting. Takata is already dissenting for 1.25% and Tamura wants a neutral ~2%.

A hold at 0% is universally expected, with panellists seeing no change until 2027 and July CPI at 0.4% undershooting the Bank's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. The relevance is language: the June statement pledged to lean against rapid franc APPRECIATION only, and any hardening of that is the main cap on how far EUR/CHF and USD/CHF can run.

geopolitics: The gap between what Washington announced and what Tehran confirmed is the whole trade today. Trump called off the strikes he had promised for the weekend after Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE urged restraint, said a deal was 'imminent' and announced that US-Iran negotiations covering the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT' would resume Monday. Iran's foreign ministry then contradicted him on the record. Spokesman Baghaei: 'We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz.' Foreign Minister Araghchi told cabinet members that the Oman-mediated negotiations are 'in their final stages' and 'on the way to being finalized' - while stating explicitly that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait. The context is a June memorandum of understanding between the two sides that allowed a temporary 60-day reopening and committed both to talks toward another nuclear agreement; the strait itself has been effectively closed since the war began on Feb 28, and when traffic briefly flowed in early July WTI traded below $70. The FX transmission runs in three channels and today all three are mispriced in the same direction. First, crude: WTI fell 7.4% to about $78 and Brent to $83.88 on Monday, the sharpest single session of 2026, as traders unwound supply-disruption hedges built up through the escalation. That was priced off the maximal version of the deal, which is not what Iran says is on the table - so the structural short in USOIL is still correct but comes off HIGH to LOW-MED conviction, with a close above $84 as the invalidation. Second, the terms-of-trade channel into CAD and NZD: the loonie has no rates leg at all with both BoC core measures under target, so it is a levered oil play and took the full hit, while the RBNZ has explicitly credited the earlier partial reopening with easing its own inflation outlook. Third, the inflation channel into the ECB: roughly 70% of a September hike is priced and that pricing was built on the oil surge Lagarde named as an upside risk, so a real reopening deflates the euro's only hawkish leg - but a denial means it may not. The tape is already signalling scepticism. Gold closed higher at $4,052 and silver at $58.26 despite a firmer dollar, which is not how a haven complex behaves when a war is genuinely ending. Keep the de-escalation trades on, size them smaller, and treat an oil snapback rather than a further collapse as the live tail.
